topicName: Modules, Mixins, and Method Lookup Path
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Modules, Mixins, and Method Lookup Path in Ruby on Rails"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"In Ruby, multiple inheritance is not supported directly through classes to avoid complexity and ambiguity like the Diamond Problem. Instead, Ruby uses modules and mixins to share behavior across different classes. Understanding how modules work and how Ruby traverses the method lookup path is essential for writing clean, maintainable Rails applications."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"What is a Module?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A module is a collection of methods, constants, and other module and class definitions. Unlike classes, modules cannot be instantiated. They serve two primary purposes in Ruby: namespaces and mixins."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"module Authenticatable
  def current_user
    @current_user ||= User.find_by(id: session[:user_id])
  end
end"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"Mixins: include, extend, and prepend"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you include a module in a class, its methods become available as instance methods. This process is called mixing in a module. Ruby provides three keywords to mix in modules:"},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"include: Adds the module's methods as instance methods of the class, placed just above the class itself in the lookup path."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"extend: Adds the module's methods as class methods (singleton methods) rather than instance methods."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"prepend: Similar to include, but places the module below the class in the lookup path, allowing its methods to override the class's own instance methods."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
  include Authenticatable
end"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"The Method Lookup Path"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you call a method on an object, Ruby searches for it along a specific chain called the method lookup path (or ancestors chain). You can inspect this path for any class by calling the ancestors method."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"puts Post.ancestors"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"The typical order in the lookup path from bottom to top is: the class itself, any prepended modules (in reverse order of prepending), included modules (in reverse order of inclusion), superclasses, and finally Object, Kernel, and BasicObject."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Practical Rails Example: Concerns"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Rails provides ActiveSupport::Concern to make writing and organizing mixins cleaner. Concerns handle dependencies and allow you to define both class and instance methods within a single module file easily."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"module Visible
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    scope :visible, -> { where(hidden: false) }
  end

  class_methods do
    def count_visible
      visible.count
    end
  end

  def hide!
    update(hidden: true)
  end
end

class Article < ApplicationRecord
  include Visible
end"},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"By mastering modules, mixins, and the method lookup path, you can keep your Rails models and controllers DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) while avoiding naming collisions and unexpected method overriding behaviors."}]
